analysis.one_liner: Protects about 24 million acres of Northern Rockies public land as wilderness, parks, and wildlife corridors.
analysis.headline: A bill to protect roughly 24 million acres of Northern Rockies public land as wilderness and wildlife corridors died in committee without a hearing, despite 185 House cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have protected the largest remaining wild region in the lower 48 states. It would have designated about 15.5 million acres of federal land in Idaho, Montana, Wyoming, Oregon, and Washington as wilderness — land where logging, mining, drilling, and road-building are prohibited — plus another 5 million acres of connecting wilderness and 3.5 million acres of managed corridors that link the ecosystems so wildlife can move between them. It would have created a new Hells Canyon national park and preserve, protected river segments, funded a restoration corps to repair damaged land, and recognized Blackfeet treaty and religious rights in the Badger-Two Medicine area. Private land would not have been affected. The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Resources Committee and its subcommittees until that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The public gains permanently protected wilderness, clean water from the headwaters of two-thirds of North America's rivers, and habitat for endangered species like grizzly bears, wolves, and caribou, along with expanded opportunities for fishing, hunting, hiking, and river recreation. Hells Canyon would gain a national park and preserve, damaged wildlands would get federally funded restoration work, and Native Americans — particularly the Blackfeet Nation — would gain formal protection of treaty and religious rights on designated lands. Taxpayers also gain on paper: the bill's own findings state the undeveloped areas are worth more left intact than the Treasury would earn from logging them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hikers, hunters, anglers, and the Blackfeet Nation

how_it_helps.text: Designates as wilderness the roadless cores of five Northern Rockies ecosystems — Greater Glacier, Greater Yellowstone, Greater Salmon/Selway, Greater Cabinet/Yaak/Selkirk, and the island mountain ranges — about 15.5 million acres in total, protecting habitat for grizzly bears, gray wolves, caribou, and salmon.

Adds roughly 5 million more acres of wilderness and 3.5 million acres of 'special corridor management areas' connecting those ecosystems, where logging, mining, oil and gas drilling, and new road construction would be prohibited and road density driven toward zero.

Creates the Hells Canyon/Chief Joseph National Park and Preserve, designates wild and scenic river segments in Idaho, Montana, and Wyoming, and establishes a Wildland Recovery Corps to restore damaged lands — putting people to work on restoration.

Recognizes Blackfeet treaty and religious rights in the Badger-Two Medicine area by designating the Blackfeet Wilderness and withdrawing it from mining and mineral leasing, and guarantees Native Americans nonexclusive access to designated areas for traditional cultural and religious purposes.
Leaves all private land untouched: the bill states it does not affect lands in private ownership, and adjacent landowners participate only voluntarily.

analysis.who_pays: Timber, mining, and oil and gas companies would lose access to millions of acres of federal land, and the workers and rural communities that depend on logging and extraction contracts would bear the adjustment. Motorized recreation users and any proposed ski or resort development in the designated areas would also be excluded. The federal government would take on the cost of restoration work and managing the new protected areas.
analysis.who_pays_short: Timber, mining, and oil and gas companies

drawbacks.text: The bill would permanently bar logging, mining, oil and gas development, and new road construction on roughly 24 million acres of federal land in five states, which would cost jobs in timber towns and reduce revenue from commodity production on public lands.

Wilderness designation under the Wilderness Act prohibits motorized vehicles and mechanical equipment, so snowmobilers, off-road users, and some existing forest users would lose access to areas they can reach today; the bill also counts ski resort facilities among the 'development' it prohibits.

Most cosponsors came from outside the affected states, and the region's main economic interests and many of its representatives opposed turning so much land over to non-development status, arguing decisions of this size should have local buy-in.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The conservation benefit is large and permanent: clean-water headwaters, habitat for endangered species, and public recreation across a region with no comparable wild landscape south of Canada, all on federal land already owned by the public. The costs are real but narrower: logging, mining, and energy companies and some rural workers in the region would lose access to public timber and minerals, and wilderness rules would bar motorized recreation and new ski development on designated land. The bill's own findings argue the undeveloped areas are worth more to the nation standing than as timber, and note that continuing roadless-area development means the public funds the loss of wilderness and water quality with its own tax dollars. Private land is expressly untouched. The main design weakness is political rather than substantive: with 43% of the House signed on but almost no support from members who represent the affected states, the bill was never positioned to move.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Resources Committee and three of its subcommittees in March 2003, no hearing or vote was ever scheduled, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 5, 2003 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Resources.

A week later it was split among three subcommittees — National Parks, Forests and Forest Health, and Fisheries Conservation, Wildlife and Oceans — and the departments of Agriculture and the Interior were asked for their views; that is the last action the record shows.

Support was substantial on paper: 185 House members cosponsored, including 167 Democrats, 17 Republicans, and 1 Independent, but the bill never reached a hearing, a committee vote, or the House floor.
The 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 with the bill still sitting in committee, and it carried over to no law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Timber, mining, and oil and gas interests kept their access to the region's public lands, and the committee leadership avoided ever having to hold a vote on a bill with 185 cosponsors.

for.name: Rep. Christopher Shays
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a large bipartisan cosponsor list.

for.name: 17 of 229 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, a small minority of their conference.

for.name: Rep. Bernard Sanders
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as the chamber's sole Independent.

against.name: Rep. Richard Pombo
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee the bill was referred to; no hearing or markup of the bill was ever scheduled during the two-year Congress, according to the action history.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Democratic — 167 of 205 House Democrats signed on versus 17 of 229 Republicans — and the Republican-controlled Resources Committee never allowed the bill a hearing or vote.

industries.note: Wilderness and corridor designations would bar timber harvest across roughly 24 million acres of federal forest, eliminating access to some of the last large roadless timber in the lower 48. The bill's own findings say most of these lands are of marginal timber value and cost more to log than they return to the Treasury.

The bill prohibits mining in the connecting corridors and withdraws the Blackfeet Wilderness from the mining and mineral leasing laws, closing millions of acres of federal land to mineral entry and new claims.
Exploration and development would be prohibited across the wilderness areas and corridor management areas, locking energy companies out of federal acreage in five Rocky Mountain states.

Permanent protected status for popular wild lands supports fishing, hunting, hiking, and river recreation economies, and the bill's restoration program would fund new recovery work. The bill explicitly cites primitive recreation and inspiration as purposes for all Americans.

Wilderness designation bars motorized vehicles and equipment, so snowmobile and off-road users would lose access to designated areas even though the bill exempts all existing highways and county roads and keeps ordinary access intact elsewhere.
